Disability Ethics

Introduction to Bioethics

Published

October 27, 2026

Today’s questions

  1. What is a disability?
  2. What, if anything, is bad about having a disability?
  3. What do the answers to (1) and (2) imply for health care?


Three models of disability:

  • The medical(-misfortune) model
  • The social(-creationist) model
  • The Barnes model (Barnes 2016)

The Medical Model of Disability

“On the Medical Model, disadvantages are natural and inevitable outcomes of simple biomedical facts. Reductions of these natural disadvantages can be accomplished only by individual cures (changing the biomedical facts) or by charitable donations intended to compensate the victims of disability for their inevitable and pitiable conditions…The Medical Model is an individualistic rather than a social theory. Disabilities are properties of individuals, and remedies (e.g., cures, rehabilitations, charitable donations) are meted out one individual at a time.” (Amundson 2005)


The Medical(-misfortune) Model of Disability

  • Disabilities are biological properties of individual bodies.
  • They are (negative) departures from “normal species functioning”
  • Ethically, they are bodily pathologies that underwrite claim to social assistance.

The Social Model of Disability

“[The social model] reconceptualizes our understanding of ‘handicapping condition,’ transforming this notion from a state of a minority of people which naturally disadvantages them in society to a state of society which artificially disadvantages a minority of people.” (Silvers 1994)


The Social(-creationist) Model of Disability

  • Disabilities are mismatches between an impaired body and a socially created environment.
  • People are disabled by an ableist society, not by their bodies.
  • Disabilities are social pathologies that underwrite complaints of injustice.

“[A]bleism is the process of favoring, fetishizing, and building the world around a mostly imagined, idealized body while discriminating against those bodies perceived to move, see, hear, process, operate, look, or need differently from that vision.” (Taussig 2020, p. 10)


Much of the time, pushing back against ableism and discrimination “feels like getting out a toothbrush to clean a filthy house when I’m still trying to find a way to breathe in these rooms full of toxic fumes.” (Taussig 2020, p. 223)

The Americans with Disabilities Act

NPR on Instagram, July 12, 2024 (click here)


“[The ADA] is especially far reaching in that it reconceptualizes our understanding of ‘handicapping condition,’ transforming this notion from a state of a minority of people which naturally disadvantages them in society to a state of society which artificially disadvantages a minority of people.” (Silvers 1994)

The Medical(-misfortune) Model of Disability

  • Disabilities are biological properties of individual bodies.
  • They are (negative) departures from “normal species functioning”
  • Ethically, they are bodily pathologies that underwrite claims to social assistance.

The Social(-creationist) Model of Disability

  • Disabilities are mismatches between an impaired body and a socially created environment.
  • People are disabled by an ableist society, not by their bodies.
  • Disabilities are therefore social pathologies that underwrite complaints of injustice.


“Disabled person” vs. “Person with disability”

Taussig, Youtube interview:


“I use identity-first language—‘disabled person’. I think person-first language has been accepted as the ‘correct’ way to talk about disabled people for a while. But I think that’s beginning to shift…


“For me, it’s because disability is part of my identity. To separate me and my disability feels inauthentic to me…My main takeaway is to listen to people describe themselves. Some people might prefer person-first language…

Shakespeare

“Disability politics has explicitly followed precedents established by civil rights, feminist and lesbian and gay liberation thinking…Despite the value in such analogies, there are limitations to the parallel.” (p. 424)



Limitations, according to Shakespeare:

  • The historical experience of race, gender and sexuality “can be explained in terms of unfair discrimination or restriction of negative freedom.” (p. 424)
  • While disabled people have certainly experienced similar treatment, they also “experience intrinsic limitations, to varying degrees, by virtue of the impairments of body or mind which are an inextricable part of being disabled.” (p. 424)
  • But compare what’s needed to nuture and protect negative liberty.

Shakespeare

  • Shakespeare’s position seems to be a sort of hybrid medical/social model of disability.



“In the case of gender, race or sexuality, there is no pathology associated with that form of embodiment and no inferiority of functioning which restricts independence and participation. For the emancipation of disabled people, it is not sufficient to remove social barriers. It is also important to provide additional support and investment.” (p. 424)

A third model

Some observations:

  • My nearsightedness may be an impairment, but it’s not a disability (which is a problem for the medical model)
  • Homosexuality may be a statistical “departure from normal species functioning”, but it’s neither an impairment nor a disability (which is a problem for the medical model)
  • It is not uncommon for disabled people to use “disability” to refer to bodily states (but this runs counter to the “pure” social model, which distinguishes between impairment and disability)
  • It is not uncommon for disabled people to celebrate and take pride in their disabilities (but this runs counter to the social model, which casts disability as the bad/unjust dimension of the body-society-environment nexus)
  • Even when disabilities involve the lack of intrinsically valuable abilities, it doesn’t follow that they are bad all-things-considered. Many disabled people say their disabilities positively enhance their well-being on balance (but this runs counter both the medical and social models, which casts disabilities as bad things to be prevented and/or redressed).

Barnes’s Model

Elizabeth Barnes argues that:

  • Disabilities are features of bodies.
    • There is no meaningful distinction between impairment and disability.
  • A bodily feature is a disability just in case it is the sort of feature “the disability rights movement is promoting justice for” (Barnes 2016, p. 43).
  • Even taken as features of bodies (rather than body-environment interactions), disabilities are “mere-differences”, not bad-differences.

Barnes’s Model


“The mere-difference view can maintain that the very same thing that causes you to lose out on some goods (unique to non-disability) allows you to participate in other goods (perhaps unique to disability). For example, the mere-difference view can grant that the ability to hear is an intrinsic good. And it’s an intrinsic good that Deaf people lack. But being Deaf is not simply the lack of the ability to hear. There are other goods, perhaps other intrinsic goods—the unique experience of language had by those whose first language is a signed rather than spoken language, the experience of music via vibrations, etc.—experienced by Deaf people and not by hearing people. Deafness can involve the lack of an intrinsic good without being merely the lack of an intrinsic good.” (Barnes 2016, p. 57)

Barnes’s Model

What’s the argument?

  • Argument from analogies:
    • the mere-difference view of sex
    • the mere-difference view of sexual orientation.
  • Argument from epistemic (in)justice:

“[M]any disabled people assure us that there are plenty of interesting, valuable, enjoyable things about living in a disabled body. There are unique experiences not had by the non-disabled, which disabled people value. The mere-difference view needn’t deny that disabled people miss out on some intrinsically good abilities or experiences—it’s just that they have access to other, different good things.” (Barnes 2016, p. 58)

Preventing Disability, Preventing Disabled People

  • Disability can be a local harm for an individual, even if it’s not a global harm. (Mere-difference view)
  • Parents have duties to prevent serious and substantial local harms to their children.

Barnes:

  • When prospective parents select against disability—for example, by selective abortion or selective implantation—they are not preventing local harms to a specific child, because when you prevent local harms in this way, you prevent the person from existing in the first place.
  • So all negative selection does is “display[] false and disparaging views of disability…[It] relies on the notion that disability is somehow sub-optimal, making an able-bodied child preferable to a child with a disability.” (Barnes 2009, p. 14)
  • That does not mean it is impermissible; but it is blameworthy.
    • A possible rule ethics/virtue ethics combo
